statement: A physical perimeter is defined for each site in scope, such as the building, floor or server room, stating the protection each one needs. At least once a cycle, the perimeters are confirmed to exist as described, for example that doors lock and there are no unprotected openings. Where the organization has no premises of its own, this is recorded and reliance is placed on the hosting provider's assurance. This keeps unauthorized people away from the areas that hold information and assets.
why_asked: Without defined perimeters, nobody can say which areas need protection, so sensitive spaces end up as open as the rest of the building.
how_to_ask: Ask for the site list and the perimeter definition for each site. Then ask whether anyone has walked the sites to confirm the perimeters match the paper. Example probe: "When did someone last walk the server room boundary and check that every door and opening is secured as the plan says?"
question: Does your organization protect the areas holding its information with defined physical perimeters?
expected_evidence: Site plans and perimeter definitions for each site in scope; site walkthrough notes or photos; for hosted environments, the provider's physical assurance reports; the record of which sites are in scope. Cover the current review period.
good_looks_like: A written perimeter definition exists for every in-scope site, naming the protection required for each area. Walkthrough records or photos show the perimeters match the definition. Sites hosted entirely by a provider are recorded as such, backed by the provider's assurance report.
test: Select a sample of in-scope sites or areas and compare each perimeter definition with a walkthrough record or photo. Pass if every sampled perimeter is defined, matches what was observed, and no unprotected opening is found. For provider-hosted sites, pass if the scope record shows reliance on a current provider assurance report.
baseline_risk: Unauthorized people could reach areas that hold information and equipment without meeting any barrier.
applicability: Applies in full where the organization runs premises that are in scope. Where all hosting is with providers, the organization records this and relies on provider assurance.

statement: Entry to each secure area is controlled through locks, badge readers or reception checks, with written rules on who may enter. Entry rules are stricter for areas holding higher-risk assets. Every visitor is recorded and escorted where the rules require. Visitor logs and access system records prove that only authorized people and recorded visitors enter.
why_asked: Without entry rules and visitor records, unauthorized people or unrecorded visitors can reach sensitive areas unnoticed.
how_to_ask: Ask how people get into the secure areas and how visitors are signed in and escorted. Example probe: "Show me this week's visitor log for the server room and tell me who escorted each visitor."
question: Does your organization control entry to its secure areas, with visitors recorded and escorted?
expected_evidence: Entry control rules for secure areas; list of secure areas and who may enter each; visitor logs; access control system reports; data center provider attestation for cloud-hosted assets. Cover the review period.
good_looks_like: Entry rules define who may enter each secure area and how, with stricter controls for higher-risk areas. Visitor logs are complete and show escorts where required. Access system records match the rules.
test: Sample visitor entries and access system records from the review period, across at least two secure areas. Pass if entry rules exist for each area, and every sampled visitor is logged and escorted as the rules require.
baseline_risk: Unauthorized people or unrecorded visitors could walk into secure areas unnoticed.

statement: Physical measures for offices, rooms and facilities are specified, such as locks, restricted signage and no public indication of where sensitive rooms are. At least once per assessment cycle, these measures are checked to be in place in the rooms holding sensitive information or equipment. This reduces the chance that sensitive rooms are found, entered or observed by people with no need.
why_asked: Sensitive rooms often get the same treatment as ordinary offices, which leaves obvious and easy targets.
how_to_ask: Ask which rooms hold sensitive information or equipment and what measures each one has. Example probe: "Which rooms would hurt most if a stranger walked in, and what stops that today?"
question: Does your organization put physical security measures in place for the offices, rooms and facilities that hold sensitive information or equipment?
expected_evidence: Physical security specification for offices and rooms; list of rooms holding sensitive information or equipment; room inspection records. Cover the current review period.
good_looks_like: A specification sets measures per room type. Inspection records show sensitive rooms meet it, with gaps tracked to closure.
test: Select a sample of rooms holding sensitive information or equipment and compare each with the specification, using inspection records or a walkthrough. Pass if every sampled room has the specified measures in place.
baseline_risk: Sensitive rooms are exposed to casual entry, observation or theft.

statement: Monitoring for unauthorized physical access to premises is in place, using CCTV, intruder alarms or guards, with a defined response when an alert fires. The monitoring systems work throughout the period and are tested on a defined cycle. Alert and test records show that monitoring ran and that alerts were acted on.
why_asked: Monitoring that is defined but not working gives false comfort, and intrusions go unseen or unanswered.
how_to_ask: Ask what monitoring exists, who responds, and how the organization knows it is working. Example probe: "If the alarm at the main entrance fired at night, who would be called and when was that last tested?"
question: Does your organization monitor its premises for unauthorized physical access and act on alerts?
expected_evidence: Physical monitoring arrangements and response responsibilities; CCTV retention settings; alarm test records; guard logs; alert and response records. Cover the review period.
good_looks_like: Monitoring covers the defined premises. A named role responds to alerts. Test and maintenance records show systems were operating all period, and any outage was fixed and recorded.
test: Pick a sample of monitoring systems and dates in the period. Pass if each sampled system has a test or log record showing it was operational, footage or logs are available for the sampled dates, and sampled alerts show a recorded response.
baseline_risk: Physical intrusions would go undetected or unanswered.

statement: Physical and environmental threats are assessed for each in-scope site, such as fire, flood, power surge and civil unrest, and the protection the assessment calls for is installed. That protection is maintained and tested on a defined cycle, and the certificates are kept. This lowers the chance that a natural event or attack on a site destroys information or equipment.
why_asked: Without a site-level assessment, protection is guesswork and the likely hazards go unprotected.
how_to_ask: Ask for the threat assessment per site and then for proof the protection it asks for is installed and current. Example probe: "What does your assessment say about flooding at the data room, and what is installed because of it?"
question: Does your organization protect each site against the physical threats it faces?
expected_evidence: Physical and environmental threat assessment for each in-scope site; risk assessment extracts; maintenance and test certificates for fire suppression, water detection and similar protection. Cover the review period.
good_looks_like: Each site has a documented assessment covering the likely hazards. Protective measures named in it are installed, and maintenance or test records are current.
test: Select a sample of sites and compare each assessment with the installed protection. Pass if a documented assessment exists for every sampled site, each protection it identifies is installed, and maintenance or test records are current.
baseline_risk: A fire, flood or power event could destroy information and equipment with no protection in place.

statement: Rules for working in secure areas are documented, for example no unsupervised third parties, no recording devices and areas locked when vacant. Authorized people are made aware of the rules through a briefing or signed acknowledgement before they get access. This keeps behavior inside secure areas consistent and defensible.
why_asked: People with access to secure areas often do not know what is expected of them while inside.
how_to_ask: Ask for the written rules and how people with access are told about them. Example probe: "What does a new engineer with data-center access sign or hear before their first entry?"
question: Does your organization set rules for working in secure areas and make sure authorized people know them?
expected_evidence: Secure area working rules; briefing records or signed acknowledgements; list of people authorized for secure areas. Cover the review period.
good_looks_like: Written rules cover supervision, devices and locking. Each authorized person has a briefing record or acknowledgement on file.
test: Sample people on the authorized list for secure areas. Pass if the rules are documented and each sampled person has a briefing record or signed acknowledgement dated no later than their access.
baseline_risk: People could behave unsafely in secure areas without knowing it, or without any basis for action.

statement: Clear desk and clear screen rules are set for papers, removable media and unattended screens. Automatic screen lock after inactivity is enforced by configuration. Compliance is spot-checked on a defined cycle and findings are followed up until closed. This stops information being read or taken from untended desks and screens.
why_asked: Policies alone do not stop information being left on desks and open screens, so the rules need both configuration and checks.
how_to_ask: Ask for the policy, the screen lock setting and the last spot-check. Example probe: "How do you know people actually lock their screens and clear their desks, not just that the policy says so?"
question: Does your organization enforce rules that stop papers, removable media and unattended screens from exposing information?
expected_evidence: Clear desk and clear screen policy; device management policy export showing the screen lock setting; spot-check records and follow-up actions. Cover the review period.
good_looks_like: The policy defines rules for papers, removable media and screens. Screen lock is enforced by configuration on endpoints. Spot-checks happen on a cycle, and findings have owners and closure dates.
test: Review the policy, then sample endpoints from the management export and sample spot-check records for the period. Pass if the policy exists, every sampled endpoint has screen lock enforced, and spot-check findings were followed up.
baseline_risk: Information could be read, copied or stolen from unattended desks and screens.

statement: Siting requirements for equipment are defined, for example servers in locked racks or rooms, screens not overlooked and protection from environmental hazards. On a defined cycle, inspection confirms that sampled equipment locations meet the requirements. This reduces environmental damage and unauthorized access to equipment.
why_asked: Equipment placed for convenience can be exposed to water, heat, theft or shoulder-surfing.
how_to_ask: Ask for the siting requirements and the latest inspection of equipment locations. Example probe: "Can I see where your network switches and servers sit, and the inspection that says that is acceptable?"
question: Does your organization site its equipment so it is safe from hazards and tampering?
expected_evidence: Equipment siting requirements; equipment location inspection records. Cover the review period.
good_looks_like: Requirements say where equipment must and must not sit. Inspection records show locations meet them, with exceptions corrected.
test: Select a sample of equipment locations and inspect or review inspection records. Pass if every sampled location meets the siting requirements.
baseline_risk: Equipment is exposed to environmental damage, tampering or theft.
applicability: Applies where the organization has equipment on premises of its own.

statement: Rules for protecting assets taken off premises are set, such as not leaving them unattended, carrying them as hand luggage and getting authorization to remove them. Full-disk encryption and remote wipe are enforced on portable devices used off-site through device management, and the compliance report is reviewed on a defined cycle. This keeps information safe if a device is lost or stolen.
why_asked: Portable devices are lost often, and an unencrypted device without remote wipe turns a lost laptop into a data breach.
how_to_ask: Ask for the rules and the device compliance report. Example probe: "If a laptop is stolen from a car tonight, what stops the thief reading it and who can wipe it?"
question: Does your organization protect assets that leave its premises, including encryption and remote wipe on portable devices?
expected_evidence: Off-premises asset rules; device management compliance report showing encryption and remote wipe status; authorization records for removing assets. Cover the review period.
good_looks_like: Rules are written and known. Every portable device in use has full-disk encryption and remote wipe enabled, and exceptions are approved and tracked.
test: Sample portable devices from the inventory and check each against the compliance report. Pass if the rules exist and every sampled device has full-disk encryption and remote wipe enabled, or an approved exception.
baseline_risk: Lost or stolen devices expose the information stored on them.
applicability: Applies if staff or contractors take assets or portable devices off premises.

statement: Critical facilities are protected against power and other utility failures through measures such as UPS, generators or redundant feeds. Maintenance and test records are kept for that equipment, and it is tested on a defined cycle. This keeps processing running, or shuts it down safely, when a utility fails.
why_asked: An untested UPS or generator fails when it is needed, and a utility failure can corrupt data or stop the business.
how_to_ask: Ask which facilities are critical, what protects their power, cooling and telecoms, and when it was last tested. Example probe: "When did you last run the generator under load and where is that record?"
question: Does your organization protect its critical facilities from power and other utility failures?
expected_evidence: Utility protection design for critical facilities; maintenance and test records for UPS, generators and cooling; continuity plan extracts. Cover the review period.
good_looks_like: Each critical facility has defined protection for power, cooling and telecoms. UPS and generator equipment has current maintenance and test records, and failures are fixed and recorded.
test: Select a sample of critical facilities and their protection equipment. Pass if protection is defined for each, and each sampled item has a maintenance or test record that is current for the period.
baseline_risk: A power or utility outage could stop operations or damage equipment and data.
applicability: Applies where the organization runs critical facilities of its own.

statement: Protection requirements for power, data and communications cabling are defined, for example conduits or locked cabinets, separation of power and data, and patch panels in secured rooms. On a defined cycle, inspection confirms that sampled cabling and communications rooms meet them. This reduces tapping, interference and accidental damage.
why_asked: Exposed cabling can be tapped or cut, and shared routes let power interfere with data.
how_to_ask: Ask for the cabling requirements and the latest inspection of communications rooms. Example probe: "Can we look at the patch panels and tell me who can reach them?"
question: Does your organization protect its cabling from interception, interference or damage?
expected_evidence: Cabling protection requirements; inspection records for sampled cabling and communications rooms. Cover the review period.
good_looks_like: Requirements address routing, separation and access to patch panels. Inspections confirm they are met, with findings fixed.
test: Select a sample of cabling runs and communications rooms. Pass if each sampled item meets the written requirements on inspection.
baseline_risk: Network or power cabling could be tapped, damaged or interfered with.
applicability: Applies where the organization has cabling or communications rooms of its own.

statement: Maintenance requirements and schedules are defined for in-scope equipment, following supplier recommendations. Only authorized personnel carry out maintenance. Maintenance records show the work was done on schedule and by whom, which keeps equipment reliable.
why_asked: Unmaintained equipment fails, and unauthorized people working on equipment can damage it or tamper with it.
how_to_ask: Ask for the maintenance schedule and the latest maintenance records. Example probe: "Show me the last scheduled service on the main storage array and who carried it out."
question: Does your organization maintain its in-scope equipment on a schedule through authorized personnel?
expected_evidence: Equipment maintenance schedules; maintenance records showing who performed the work; list of authorized maintenance personnel or vendors; asset inventory extract. Cover the review period.
good_looks_like: Schedules exist for all in-scope equipment and follow supplier recommendations. Records show work done on time and only by authorized personnel.
test: Sample equipment from the inventory and the maintenance records for the review period. Pass if each sampled item has a defined schedule and its maintenance was done on schedule by an authorized person.
baseline_risk: Equipment fails unexpectedly or is tampered with during unauthorized maintenance.

statement: Who holds physical access to secure areas is reviewed on a defined cycle, and any access no longer needed is removed. When a person leaves, their badges and keys are deactivated or collected and the removal is recorded. Review records and leaver removal records prove that access rights stay current.
why_asked: Access rights pile up over time, and former staff can keep badges or keys that still open secure areas.
how_to_ask: Ask when the access lists were last checked against current staff and how leavers' badges are handled. Example probe: "Take the last person who left and show me when their badge stopped working."
question: Does your organization review physical access rights on a defined cycle and remove access for leavers?
expected_evidence: Physical access review records; access lists before and after the review; leaver list from HR; badge deactivation or key return records. Cover the review period.
good_looks_like: Access lists for each secure area are reviewed on a defined cycle, with findings actioned and recorded. Leavers' badges are deactivated or keys returned promptly, with a record that matches the leaver list.
test: Take the latest physical access review and a sample of leavers from the review period. Pass if the review is on file with findings actioned, and every sampled leaver's badge was deactivated or keys returned with a record.
baseline_risk: Former staff or people who changed roles keep physical access to secure areas.

statement: Before equipment leaves the site for repair, sensitive information on it is cleared or the equipment is otherwise protected. Each send-off is recorded with the method used. These records prove that repair vendors do not receive readable sensitive data.
why_asked: Repair vendors can read data left on devices sent out for fixing.
how_to_ask: Ask for the last equipment sent off site for repair and how its data was handled. Example probe: "The last disk that went back to the vendor, who wiped it and where is the record?"
question: Does your organization clear or protect sensitive information on equipment before it is sent off site for repair?
expected_evidence: Repair send-off records; data clearing or sanitization records; encryption or protection records for equipment sent out; vendor repair agreements. Cover the review period.
good_looks_like: Every item sent off site has a record showing its data was cleared or protected, and the method used. Where clearing is not possible, other protection is recorded.
test: Sample equipment sent off site for repair during the review period. Pass if each sampled item has a record showing sensitive information was cleared or the equipment was otherwise protected before it left.
baseline_risk: Sensitive data is exposed to repair vendors through equipment sent out unwiped.
applicability: Applies where equipment is sent off site for maintenance or repair.
